title: Alibaba plans revenue-sharing terms for big commercial users of its next open-weight Qwen model
subtitle: A Reuters exclusive says the paid tier will land alongside the open-weight release of Qwen3.8-Max in the week of August 10 — mirroring the licence Moonshot attached to Kimi K3.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Reuters reported on August 6, citing two people familiar with the plans, that Alibaba intends to require large commercial users of its next open-weight Qwen release to sign a paid agreement and share a portion of the revenue they generate from the model. The measure is expected to arrive alongside the open-weight release of Qwen3.8-Max, which the company signalled will land in the week of August 10. Alibaba unveiled Qwen3.8-Max — a 2.4-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts model with roughly 95 billion active parameters and a one-million-token context window — on August 3. Weights for the base model have been released to Hugging Face and ModelScope; the licensing change applies to what commercial deployments look like on top of them. The specific revenue-share percentage and the annual-revenue threshold that triggers negotiations have not been finalised, and the story was still being picked up across TechNode, Yahoo Finance, and Quartz through August 8.

The design copies Moonshot AI, whose Kimi K3 licence requires any party that resells Kimi K3 as a service and clears $20 million in annual revenue from it to enter a commercial agreement — one that can include revenue sharing of up to 30%. Both companies are threading the needle between two things they want at once: the reach and developer goodwill that open weights deliver, and a path to monetise the very largest downstream users who would otherwise self-host at no cost to Alibaba. Individual developers, academics, and small companies can still run Qwen3.8-Max locally under the standard open-weight terms; the paid tier only bites at the top of the usage curve. Alibaba is not framing the shift as a retreat from open source. It is framing it as commercial hygiene at scale.

The move is the clearest sign yet that the Chinese open-weight ecosystem is diverging from the Meta-Llama template that defined the space in 2024 and 2025. Llama's community licence permits commercial use up to a 700-million monthly-active-user cap, above which Meta requires a bespoke agreement — a threshold few companies ever cross. Alibaba's and Moonshot's terms lower that trigger by orders of magnitude, which means the number of downstream companies that will actually have to negotiate a licence goes from 'a handful of hyperscalers' to 'any AI-first company with real revenue.' The strategic bet is that as the Chinese frontier catches or exceeds the U.S. frontier — Qwen3.8-Max is competitive with Kimi K3, GPT-5.6, and Claude Opus 5 on public benchmarks — commercial users will pay for the assurance of a real licence rather than take the legal risk of a permissive-in-name-only clause.

For learners: 'open source' in AI is now a spectrum, not a binary. Before you build on any open-weight model, read its licence — specifically the field-of-use clauses, the revenue thresholds, the redistribution rules, and what happens when the vendor updates the terms on a future version. The Open Source Initiative's OSAID 1.0 definition is a useful yardstick; almost none of today's flagship 'open' model licences meet it. That is not automatically a problem for your use case, but it is a fact you should discover before you have shipped a product on top of the weights, not after.
